1.title: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy
1.context: Letters in the ancient world named their senders first. Silvanus is Silas’s fuller Roman name; all three men had stood in Thessalonica, and all three sign a letter to a church none of them could currently visit.
1.question: Who would co-sign the most important letter of your life, and why them?

1.title: Faith, Love, Hope
1.context: The triad faith, love, and hope runs through Paul’s letters, most famously in 1 Corinthians 13. Here each carries a verb: faith works, love labors, hope endures.
1.question: Which of the three is strongest in you right now, and which most needs to grow?

1.title: Not Only in Word
1.context: Chosen and beloved frame the founding as God’s act before it was the missionaries’. The evidence Paul cites is double: the Spirit’s power among the hearers, and the team’s own life lived in front of them.
1.question: Where have you seen a message carry power because of the life of the person who brought it?

1.title: Imitators and an Example
1.context: Macedonia and Achaia were the two Roman provinces of northern and southern Greece. The new church’s faith became regional news within months of its founding, while it was still under pressure at home.
1.question: Who is imitating your faith, whether you asked them to or not?

1.title: Turned, Serving, Waiting
1.context: Thessalonica was a port city full of cults and emperor worship. Turned to God from idols is the letter’s one-sentence summary of conversion, and awaiting the Son is the posture the whole letter returns to.
1.question: What have you turned from, and what are you learning to wait for?

2.title: Not in Vain
2.context: Philippi’s story is in Acts 16: beaten, jailed, and released, the team traveled some hundred miles to Thessalonica and preached again. Paul treats the wounds as credentials, not embarrassments.
2.question: What hardship in your past has become part of your credibility?

2.title: Approved by God
2.context: Traveling teachers in the ancient world often lived on fees and flattery, and were suspected accordingly. Paul answers the suspicion by inviting God as witness to his accounts and his motives.
2.question: Whose examination of your motives do you actually trust?

2.title: A Nursing Mother
2.context: Paul worked a trade, traditionally read as tentmaking from Acts 18:3, to avoid charging new converts. Night and day labor beside the preaching is his proof that the sharing was of lives, not only of words.
2.question: Who has shared their life with you, not only their knowledge? What did it cost them?

2.title: As a Father Treats His Children
2.context: The two parental images stand as a pair: a mother’s gentleness and a father’s urging. Each of you is individual: the care was personal, not a program run on a crowd.
2.question: Who encouraged, comforted, and urged you at the right times? Whose turn is it to receive that from you?

3.title: Not as the Word of Men
3.context: The classification of a message decides what it can do. Received as God’s word rather than men’s opinion, the message is still at work in the believers, present tense, long after the speakers left.
3.question: What word are you still treating as mere opinion that asks to be received as more?

3.title: Imitators in Suffering
3.context: The Judean churches’ suffering stands behind this passage in the early chapters of Acts. Paul’s sentence about the opposition is the letter’s sharpest, and it is left here in his words, in its moment of grief over a blocked road.
3.question: How do you speak honestly about people who have hurt what you love, without letting one sentence become your whole verdict on them?

3.title: Torn Away
3.context: Torn away is a bereavement word, used of children orphaned from parents. Satan obstructed us is stated without any mechanism; the letter is interested in the fact of the blocked road, not its machinery.
3.question: What good road in your life is blocked right now, and what do you do while it stays blocked?

3.title: Our Glory and Our Joy
3.context: The crown in view is a victor’s wreath, relocated to the Lord’s coming. Paul measures his life’s success by people standing in that presence, not by any record he could display sooner.
3.question: If your crown were people, who would be standing in it?

4.title: Left on Our Own in Athens
4.context: Athens in Acts 17 is a city of idols and arguments, and Paul’s distress there stands behind this chapter. Timothy, the youngest of the team, drew the hardest assignment: go back toward the trouble.
4.question: When has sending help meant accepting loneliness yourself?

4.title: For Fear That the Tempter
4.context: The team had warned the Thessalonians persecution would come, and it came. The fear named here is not that the church would suffer, but that suffering would make the labor vain.
4.question: What labor of yours do you most fear will turn out to have been in vain?

4.title: But Just Now, Timothy Has Returned
4.context: Just now is the letter’s timestamp: the good news is fresh when Paul writes. Acts 18:5 places Silas and Timothy’s arrival from Macedonia at Corinth, which is why the series places the letter there.
4.question: What report are you waiting on that would let you go on living, in Paul’s sense?

4.title: Supply What Is Lacking
4.context: Lacking is gentle from writers this grateful: the faith is real and unfinished. The prayer that ends the chapter aims their love at the same horizon as everything else, the coming of the Lord Jesus with all his saints.
4.question: What is lacking in your faith that you would want supplied face to face, not by message?

5.title: All the More
5.context: The commendation comes first: the life being urged is the life already being lived, and the ask is growth, not rescue. Instructions given by the authority of the Lord Jesus carry the chapter’s weight.
5.question: Where are you already living rightly, and what would all the more look like there?

5.title: God’s Will: Your Holiness
5.context: Holiness in this passage is concrete and bodily, set against the sexual norms of a pagan port. The Holy Spirit is named as the one God gives, which makes rejecting the teaching a rejection of the giver.
5.question: What does holiness require of your body and habits in this season, specifically?

5.title: Taught by God to Love
5.context: Taught by God is one word in Greek, and Paul spends it on brotherly love rather than on doctrine. The love already runs province-wide; the commendation and the urge to excel arrive together.
5.question: Who taught you to love, and how would they know it took?

5.title: Aspire to Live Quietly
5.context: Aspire usually aims at honor; Paul aims it at quietness, one’s own work, and independence. In a church stirred up about the Lord’s coming, working hands are a theological statement.
5.question: What quiet, ordinary faithfulness is your ambition for this year?

6.title: Not Grieve Like the Rest
6.context: Sleep is the passage’s word for the Christian dead, and uninformed is the problem it treats. Paul does not forbid grief; he refuses it the hopelessness of those who think death ends the story.
6.question: Whose loss do you grieve, and what difference would hope make to the grieving?

6.title: God Will Bring With Jesus
6.context: Died is said of Jesus; asleep is said of believers. The distinction is the argument in miniature: his death was the real one, and his rising is why theirs is called sleep.
6.question: What do you believe about the people you love who have died, and where did that belief come from?

6.title: The Dead in Christ Will Be the First to Rise
6.context: By the word of the Lord claims an authority the letter does not explain further. The sequence answers the fear behind the passage: the dead are not at a disadvantage. They rise first, and the reunion is together.
6.question: Who do you most look forward to being together with again?

6.title: Encourage One Another With These Words
6.context: The teaching’s destination is a practice: believers comforting believers with the sequence itself. From the earliest churches this passage was read at gravesides, which is exactly the use its last verse commands.
6.question: Who needs these words from you, in person, this week?

7.title: Like a Thief in the Night
7.context: Jesus himself used the thief image for his coming in the Gospels. Paul assumes the Thessalonians were taught it in person: they are fully aware, and no schedule is owed to the fully aware.
7.question: What are you treating as schedulable that can only be lived ready for?

7.title: Peace and Security
7.context: Peace and security was the Roman Empire’s proudest slogan for what it gave the world. Paul quotes it as the lullaby of the unprepared, and answers an empire’s promise with a labor ward’s certainty.
7.question: What slogan of safety do you catch yourself trusting?

7.title: Sons of the Light
7.context: The armor here is faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet: the opening triad of the letter, worn. Isaiah’s warrior imagery stands behind the picture, reissued to a young church.
7.question: Which piece of the armor is thinnest on you right now?

7.title: Whether We Are Awake or Asleep
7.context: Awake or asleep unites the two chapters: the living watchers and the sleeping dead share one promise, to live together with him. The appointment named is salvation, not wrath.
7.question: What would change in your week if you believed your appointment is salvation, full stop?

8.title: Hold Them in Highest Regard
8.context: The leaders are known by work, care, and admonition, not by titles. Esteem because of their work keeps honor practical: it is paid to labor, not to office.
8.question: Who works diligently among you, and how could you acknowledge them this week?

8.title: Be Patient With Everyone
8.context: Three conditions get three different responses, and patience covers all of them. The ban on repaying evil for evil reaches past the congregation’s walls to all people, in a city that had given this church real evil to repay.
8.question: Who needs correction from you, who needs encouragement, and who simply needs your help? Are you sure which is which?

8.title: Test All Things
8.context: Rejoice, pray, and give thanks are called God’s will in the same terms as holiness in chapter 4. The Spirit’s fire is guarded by testing rather than by suspicion: openness and examination are commanded together.
8.question: What have you been tempted to extinguish that you should test instead?

8.title: Read to All the Brothers
8.context: The charge to read the letter aloud to all the brothers turns a courier’s page into the whole church’s possession. It is why this letter survived to be read far beyond Thessalonica, by gatherings Paul never imagined.
8.question: What word meant for you needs to be shared with the whole household, not kept in a drawer?
